html:
The third emperor of the Maurya Empire, who ruled most of the Indian subcontinent from about 268 to 232 BCE. After a brutal war he turned to Buddhism and did more than anyone to spread it across Asia.

He was the grandson of Chandragupta Maurya. In about the eighth year of his reign he conquered Kalinga on the east coast. In his own words, the Kalinga War killed a hundred thousand people and carried off a hundred and fifty thousand, and he felt deep remorse.

From then on he preached dhamma, a code of moral conduct: respect for parents and teachers, kindness to servants and animals, tolerance between religious sects, and restraint in killing. He sent officials to spread it, planted shade trees, dug wells and set up rest houses and medical care for people and animals. He announced all this in the Edicts of Ashoka, carved on rocks and polished stone pillars across his empire, in local Prakrit and in Greek and Aramaic in the northwest.

He sent Buddhist missions abroad. His son Mahinda took Buddhism to Sri Lanka, and one edict names five Greek kings to the west who received his envoys. He built or enlarged stupas, including the Great Stupa at Sanchi, and set up a pillar at Lumbini, the Buddha's birthplace.

After the empire fell he was mostly forgotten in India, though Buddhist legends kept his name. In 1837 James Prinsep deciphered the Brahmi script of the edicts and recovered his voice. The Lion Capital from his pillar at Sarnath is now India's national emblem, and his wheel of dhamma is on India's flag.
